items.prompt:
(1) Which reference is used in defining relative atomic mass?
A. The mass of one hydrogen-1 atom
B. One twelfth of a carbon-14 atom’s mass
C. The average mass of carbon atoms
D. One twelfth of a carbon-12 atom’s mass [1]

(2) What does relative formula mass represent?
A. The average of the atom masses
B. The number of atoms in the formula
C. The summed relative atomic masses
D. The formula mass measured in grams [1]

(3) Which quantity is one mole of water molecules?
A. Exactly one gram of pure water
B. Approximately 6.022 × 10²³ hydrogen atoms
C. One individual molecule of pure water
D. Approximately 6.022 × 10²³ H2O molecules [1]

(4) If Mr(CO2)=44, what is the mass of one mole of CO2?
A. 44 g
B. 6.022 × 10²³ g
C. 44 mol
D. 1 g [1]

(5) Which description defines an empirical formula?
A. The ratio of masses of the elements
B. The simplest whole-number atom ratio
C. The actual atom counts in a molecule
D. The simplest ratio of reaction coefficients [1]

(6) What is empirical formula mass?
A. Relative mass of the simplest formula
B. Molar mass divided by Avogadro constant
C. Mean atomic mass of its elements
D. Molecular mass divided by atom count [1]

(7) 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. What MgO mass forms from 2.4 g Mg with excess oxygen and complete conversion? Ar: Mg 24, O 16.
A. 2.4 g
B. 1.6 g
C. 40 g
D. 4.0 g [1]

(8) What amount of solute is present in 50.0 cm³ of a 0.200 mol/dm³ solution?
A. 0.0100 mol
B. 0.00400 mol
C. 10.0 mol
D. 0.250 mol [1]

(9) What volume does 0.100 mol gas occupy at room temperature and pressure using 24 dm³/mol?
A. 0.00417 dm³
B. 24.0 dm³
C. 2.40 dm³
D. 240 dm³ [1]

(10) A compound has empirical formula CH2 and Mr=42. Ar: C 12, H 1. What is its molecular formula?
A. C2H4
B. C3H6
C. CH2
D. C42H84 [1]

(11) What percentage of the mass of H2O is hydrogen? Ar: H 1, O 16.
A. 88.9%
B. 11.1%
C. 66.7%
D. 5.56% [1]

(12) What is the percentage yield when 6.0 g pure product is obtained against a theoretical 8.0 g?
A. 133%
B. 25%
C. 75%
D. 48% [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) D. One twelfth of a carbon-12 atom’s mass. Ar compares average atomic mass with the carbon-12 reference.
Distractor explanations: A: Hydrogen-1 is not the reference in the stated definition. B: The reference isotope is carbon-12, not carbon-14. C: The definition uses carbon-12 specifically, not the average of carbon isotopes.

(2) C. The summed relative atomic masses. Each atom contributes its Ar according to the formula.
Distractor explanations: A: Relative formula mass is a sum, not an average. B: Atom count ignores the different relative atomic masses. D: Relative formula mass is dimensionless, not a mass in grams.

(3) D. Approximately 6.022 × 10²³ H2O molecules. The mole counts the specified particles, here water molecules.
Distractor explanations: A: One mole of water has a mass of approximately 18 g, not 1 g. B: One mole of H2O contains two moles of hydrogen atoms. The stated hydrogen-atom count is only half of that required. C: One molecule is far less than Avogadro’s number of molecules.

(4) A. 44 g. Molar mass is numerically 44 g/mol.
Distractor explanations: B: Avogadro’s number counts particles; it is not the mass in grams. C: Moles measure amount, but the question asks for mass. D: One mole need not have a mass of one gram.

(5) B. The simplest whole-number atom ratio. An empirical formula states the simplest ratio.
Distractor explanations: A: An empirical formula uses atom or mole ratios, not mass ratios. C: Actual molecular counts define a molecular formula, which need not be simplest. D: Reaction coefficients compare reacting amounts, not the composition of one compound.

(6) A. Relative mass of the simplest formula. It sums Ar values for the empirical formula.
Distractor explanations: B: Dividing molar mass by Avogadro’s constant gives a single-particle mass. C: The elemental masses are added according to the formula, not averaged. D: Dividing by total atom count gives an average, not empirical formula mass.

(7) D. 4.0 g. 2.4/24=0.10 mol Mg gives 0.10 mol MgO; 0.10×40=4.0 g.
Distractor explanations: A: Ignores the mass of oxygen incorporated into the product. B: This is the oxygen mass added, not the total MgO mass. C: 40 g is one mole of MgO; only 0.100 mol forms.

(8) A. 0.0100 mol. 0.200×(50.0/1000)=0.0100 mol.
Distractor explanations: B: 0.00400 mol would correspond to 0.0200 dm³ at this concentration, not the stated 0.0500 dm³. C: Fails to convert cm³ to dm³ before multiplying. D: Divides volume by concentration instead of multiplying.

(9) C. 2.40 dm³. V=0.100×24=2.40 dm³ at room conditions.
Distractor explanations: A: Divides amount by molar volume instead of multiplying. B: Uses the volume of one mole rather than 0.100 mol. D: Divides molar volume by amount instead of multiplying.

(10) B. C3H6. Empirical mass 14; 42/14=3, giving C3H6.
Distractor explanations: A: The multiplier must be 42/14 = 3, not 2. C: CH2 is the empirical formula and has mass 14, not 42. D: Uses 42 as the multiplier instead of dividing by empirical formula mass.

(11) B. 11.1%. (2 ÷ 18) × 100 ≈ 11.1%.
Distractor explanations: A: 16/18 × 100 ≈ 88.9% is the oxygen mass percentage; hydrogen contributes 2/18. C: 2/3 × 100 ≈ 66.7% counts hydrogen atoms, but the requested mass fraction is 2/18. D: 1/18 × 100 ≈ 5.56% counts one H atom; H2O contains two, so use 2/18.

(12) C. 75%. 6.0/8.0=75%.
Distractor explanations: A: Inverts actual/theoretical yield. B: This is the percentage shortfall, not the yield. D: Multiplies the two masses instead of taking their ratio.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option D (1). D. One twelfth of a carbon-12 atom’s mass. Ar compares average atomic mass with the carbon-12 reference. Distractor explanations: A: Hydrogen-1 is not the reference in the stated definition. B: The reference isotope is carbon-12, not carbon-14. C: The definition uses carbon-12 specifically, not the average of carbon isotopes. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 2: Correct option C (1). C. The summed relative atomic masses. Each atom contributes its Ar according to the formula. Distractor explanations: A: Relative formula mass is a sum, not an average. B: Atom count ignores the different relative atomic masses. D: Relative formula mass is dimensionless, not a mass in grams. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 3: Correct option D (1). D. Approximately 6.022 × 10²³ H2O molecules. The mole counts the specified particles, here water molecules. Distractor explanations: A: One mole of water has a mass of approximately 18 g, not 1 g. B: One mole of H2O contains two moles of hydrogen atoms. The stated hydrogen-atom count is only half of that required. C: One molecule is far less than Avogadro’s number of molecules. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 4: Correct option A (1). A. 44 g. Molar mass is numerically 44 g/mol. Distractor explanations: B: Avogadro’s number counts particles; it is not the mass in grams. C: Moles measure amount, but the question asks for mass. D: One mole need not have a mass of one gram. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 5: Correct option B (1). B. The simplest whole-number atom ratio. An empirical formula states the simplest ratio. Distractor explanations: A: An empirical formula uses atom or mole ratios, not mass ratios. C: Actual molecular counts define a molecular formula, which need not be simplest. D: Reaction coefficients compare reacting amounts, not the composition of one compound. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 6: Correct option A (1). A. Relative mass of the simplest formula. It sums Ar values for the empirical formula. Distractor explanations: B: Dividing molar mass by Avogadro’s constant gives a single-particle mass. C: The elemental masses are added according to the formula, not averaged. D: Dividing by total atom count gives an average, not empirical formula mass. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 7: Correct option D (1). D. 4.0 g. 2.4/24=0.10 mol Mg gives 0.10 mol MgO; 0.10×40=4.0 g. Distractor explanations: A: Ignores the mass of oxygen incorporated into the product. B: This is the oxygen mass added, not the total MgO mass. C: 40 g is one mole of MgO; only 0.100 mol forms. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 8: Correct option A (1). A. 0.0100 mol. 0.200×(50.0/1000)=0.0100 mol. Distractor explanations: B: 0.00400 mol would correspond to 0.0200 dm³ at this concentration, not the stated 0.0500 dm³. C: Fails to convert cm³ to dm³ before multiplying. D: Divides volume by concentration instead of multiplying. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 9: Correct option C (1). C. 2.40 dm³. V=0.100×24=2.40 dm³ at room conditions. Distractor explanations: A: Divides amount by molar volume instead of multiplying. B: Uses the volume of one mole rather than 0.100 mol. D: Divides molar volume by amount instead of multiplying. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 10: Correct option B (1). B. C3H6. Empirical mass 14; 42/14=3, giving C3H6. Distractor explanations: A: The multiplier must be 42/14 = 3, not 2. C: CH2 is the empirical formula and has mass 14, not 42. D: Uses 42 as the multiplier instead of dividing by empirical formula mass. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 11: Correct option B (1). B. 11.1%. (2 ÷ 18) × 100 ≈ 11.1%. Distractor explanations: A: 16/18 × 100 ≈ 88.9% is the oxygen mass percentage; hydrogen contributes 2/18. C: 2/3 × 100 ≈ 66.7% counts hydrogen atoms, but the requested mass fraction is 2/18. D: 1/18 × 100 ≈ 5.56% counts one H atom; H2O contains two, so use 2/18. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 12: Correct option C (1). C. 75%. 6.0/8.0=75%. Distractor explanations: A: Inverts actual/theoretical yield. B: This is the percentage shortfall, not the yield. D: Multiplies the two masses instead of taking their ratio. No mark for more than one selected option.

items.prompt:
(a) State the meaning of amount concentration in mol/dm³. [1]

(b) Calculate the concentration of a solution containing 0.0100 mol solute in a total volume of 250 cm³. [3]

(c) Explain why adding water to a solution lowers its concentration if no solute is lost or reacts. [2]

(d) Explain why equal volumes of 0.100 mol/dm³ and 0.200 mol/dm³ NaOH require different volumes of the same HCl solution for complete neutralisation. HCl and NaOH react 1:1. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Moles of dissolved substance per dm³ of solution.

(b) V=250/1000=0.250 dm³. c=n/V=0.0100/0.250=0.0400 mol/dm³.

(c) The solute amount stays constant while total solution volume increases, so amount per unit volume decreases.

(d) At equal volume, the 0.200 mol/dm³ NaOH contains twice as many moles. It requires twice the amount of HCl by the 1:1 ratio, and therefore twice the volume of a fixed-concentration HCl solution.
marking_guidance: Part a: Moles of solute per dm³ of solution (1).
Part c: Larger volume lowers amount per volume (1).
Part d: Twice the NaOH amount at equal volume (1).
Part d: Twice the HCl amount from 1:1 ratio (1).
Part d: Twice the same-concentration HCl volume (1).

items.prompt:
(a) Name the apparatus used to deliver a measured, variable volume of HCl during a titration. [1]

(b) State the initial and final readings from the magnified burette panels in visuals/VIS-6117-4-readings.svg. The scale increases downwards and each small division is 0.1 cm³. [2]

(c) Calculate the titre and amount of HCl delivered from initial reading 0.40 cm³ and final reading 25.40 cm³. The HCl concentration is 0.100 mol/dm³. [3]

(d) Calculate the NaOH concentration if that HCl neutralises a 25.0 cm³ NaOH aliquot exactly. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. The HCl amount is 0.00250 mol; correct follow-through from part (c) is also allowed. [2]

(e) Explain why a rough titre should be followed by repeated careful titrations before choosing a mean. A rough trial used large additions near the endpoint. [2]

(f) State two conditions to keep constant across repeat titrations: one involving the NaOH sample and one involving endpoint detection. [2]

![Question stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-4-readings.svg)
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Burette.

(b) Initial 0.40 cm³; final 25.40 cm³, reading the bottom of each meniscus.

(c) Titre=25.40−0.40=25.00 cm³=0.02500 dm³. n(HCl)=cV=0.100×0.02500=0.00250 mol.

(d) The 1:1 ratio gives n(NaOH)=0.00250 mol. c=0.00250/0.0250=0.100 mol/dm³.

(e) Large additions can overshoot the endpoint, making the rough titre too high. Repeat with small additions near the endpoint, then use a mean of suitably close concordant titres rather than including the rough overshoot.

(f) Keep the NaOH aliquot volume at 25.0 cm³ and use the same indicator and endpoint criterion.
marking_guidance: Part b: Final 25.40 cm³ (1); accept each within ±0.05 cm³.
Part c: Final minus initial gives 25.00 cm³ (1).
Part c: n=cV gives 0.00250 mol (1); follow through permitted readings.
Part d: 1:1 ratio gives 0.00250 mol NaOH (1).
Part d: Divide by 0.0250 dm³ to give 0.100 mol/dm³ (1); follow through part (c).
Part e: Rough large additions can overshoot/increase uncertainty (1).
Part e: Repeat carefully and average concordant titres, excluding the rough result (1).

items.prompt:

(b) Calculate the HCl amount in 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ HCl. [2]

(c) Calculate the theoretical CO2 volume at room temperature and pressure when that HCl reacts completely with excess Na2CO3. 2HCl + Na2CO3 → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2. Molar gas volume=24 dm³/mol. The HCl amount is 0.00500 mol; correct follow-through from part (b) is allowed. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) n=cV, with V in dm³ for c in mol/dm³.

(b) V=25.0/1000=0.0250 dm³; n=0.200×0.0250=0.00500 mol.

(c) n(CO2)=0.00500/2=0.00250 mol. V=0.00250×24=0.0600 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

Part b: Volume conversion and substitution (1).
